rules.statement: Don't put EF Core migrations, a provider choice or provider-specific wiring in a published, provider-neutral persistence library; it ships the model only, and the migrations live in a host-owned database project that sets `MigrationsAssembly` to itself.
rules.why: Migrations in the published library would tie every consumer to one provider and one schema history.
rules.check: Look for a `Migrations/` folder, `UseNpgsql`/`UseSqlServer` calls or a `MigrationsAssembly` setting added to a packable library project instead of the host's database project.

rules.statement: A host must never apply EF Core migrations at startup, in any environment. A dedicated migration worker applies them and exits, and the host waits for that worker to finish.
rules.why: A migration that fails inside the API process crashes the host. A separate resource keeps the failure visible and contained.
rules.check: Look for `Database.Migrate()`, `MigrateAsync()` or a hosted service that migrates in the host's startup path, and for an orchestrator or AppHost that starts the API without `WaitForCompletion` on the migration worker.

rules.statement: Don't create or evolve a relational schema with `EnsureCreated`; use migrations.
rules.why: `EnsureCreated` can create a schema but can never change one later.
rules.check: Look for `Database.EnsureCreated()` or `EnsureCreatedAsync()` calls against a relational context.

rules.statement: Give every migrated DbContext an `IDesignTimeDbContextFactory` in its database project, so `dotnet ef` never has to boot the host.
rules.why: `dotnet ef` would otherwise start the whole host to build the context.
rules.check: When a new DbContext with migrations is added, check that its database project has a matching design-time factory.

rules.statement: Persist the ASP.NET Core Data Protection key ring with `PersistKeysToDbContext` in a host-owned context that has its own migrations history, never in a shared library's DbContext or in a file next to the database.
rules.why: A `DataProtectionKeys` table in the shared context forces that table on every consumer of the library. A file creates a second storage location that a reset has to keep in sync with the database.
rules.check: Look for `IDataProtectionKeyContext` or a `DataProtectionKeys` DbSet added to a library context, and for `PersistKeysToFileSystem` in host configuration.

rules.statement: Keep hand-written types out of a project's `Migrations/` folder, because that folder is treated as generated code.
rules.why: Everything under `Migrations/` is marked `generated_code` in `.editorconfig` and excluded from the formatter, so hand-written code there would not be analyzed or formatted.
rules.check: Look for non-migration classes, such as rules, helpers or tests, added under a `Migrations/` directory.

rules.statement: Every EF Core model change must come with its migration in the same change.
rules.why: A model change without its migration breaks the first deployment that needs it.
rules.check: The build's `dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes` drift step fails on this, so a reviewer only needs to confirm that a changed entity or configuration has a matching migration.

rules.statement: Register a health check for the host's DbContext (`AddDbContextCheck`) and tag it as a readiness check.
rules.why: The database is a dependency the host needs before it can serve traffic, so it belongs in the readiness check.
rules.check: When a host registers a relational DbContext, check for a matching `AddDbContextCheck<T>` tagged for readiness.

rules.statement: Seed data from idempotent seed handlers in the host, not from the migration worker or the migrations.
rules.why: The worker only applies the schema. Seeding has to be safe to run again on every start.
rules.check: Look for seed inserts in migrations or the migration worker, and for seed handlers that insert without first checking whether the data already exists.

rules.statement: Don't store developer state such as databases or key rings under `App_Data/` or in other local files; keep it in the orchestrated database so that one reset clears it all.
rules.why: State spread across several places can drift out of sync. Deleting one piece without the others leaves stored keys that can no longer be decrypted.
rules.check: Look for file paths under `App_Data/`, SQLite files or file-based key storage added to host configuration.
